.claude\rules\convergence-gate.md:103:**Supplementary signal — commits/day (cpd)**: raw age alone under-specifies stability. A 99-day-old repo shipping 15 commits/day is structurally different from a 99-day-old repo shipping 1 commit/week — the former is still in active iteration, not burn-in. Compute `cpd = total_commits / age_days` alongside age:
.claude\rules\convergence-gate.md:110:| `cpd > 10` AND `age < 100d` | Fast-churn anti-pattern | Treat age-PASS as borderline, expect rewrites, re-audit after +90d |
.claude\rules\convergence-gate.md:111:| **STRONG-PROVENANCE-EXPRESS** (5th band, predicate-gated): `age ≥ 30d` AND axis-1 = official-org maintainership AND axis-2 = named-T2 endorsement OR maintainer-org IS T2-equivalent | **Firm axis-3 PASS — relaxed maturity gate** | When provenance is strong (org-level T1) AND a named-T2 OR org-equivalent endorsement exists, the launch-spike risk that motivates the strict 90-day gate is dominated by maintainer-org commitment. Examples of org-level T1 patterns: vercel-labs / anthropics / openai / getzep / langchain / microsoft / google / facebook-research / google-deepmind / openai-evals / equivalents. .claude\rules\audit-action-loop.md:123:Audit-failure is the worst defect class: a broken audit looks like it's working (entries appear in JSONL) while providing 0 protection. .claude\rules\closed-loop-recursive-narrowing.md:20:When a closed-loop reviewer (codex postcommit, santa-loop, etc.) keeps finding finer-grained concerns on the **same logical surface** across rounds, you face two questions: when to stop the arc, and what disposition to ship.
.claude\rules\closed-loop-recursive-narrowing.md:38:**Critical**: stopping iteration is independent of shipping disposition. Hitting round 5 does NOT mean the surface is safe to ship — it means you've spent enough effort on layer-fix and need to switch to a terminal disposition (ACCEPT-WITH-DOC, REVERT-AND-REMOVE, or escalate to user). The terminal disposition has its OWN gates beyond iteration count.
.claude\rules\closed-loop-recursive-narrowing.md:46:ACCEPT-WITH-DOC is a **hard deny** for any unresolved `high` or `critical` codex severity. No combination of confidence trend, iteration count, or owner signoff can convert an unresolved high/critical finding into ACCEPT-WITH-DOC. (If you want to ship anyway, see the separate MANUAL-OVERRIDE disposition below.)
.claude\rules\closed-loop-recursive-narrowing.md:66:Disposition: ship a doc-comment ACCEPT in the patch site explaining threat model + verification reference + ROI + upstream issue queue. Future workers see the explicit acceptance; arc closes cleanly.
.claude\rules\closed-loop-recursive-narrowing.md:68:**Anti-example (would FAIL the severity gate)**: round 1 high (0.88) → round 2 high (0.80) → round 3 high (0.73) → "stop at round 5 ceiling, monotone-decline, ACCEPT". This would be wrong — severity stayed high; the underlying defect is still material; ACCEPT-WITH-DOC normalizes shipping known security/correctness regressions.
.claude\rules\closed-loop-recursive-narrowing.md:72:Confidence reverses between rounds on the **same concern**. This is codex saying "your disposition didn't address my actual point" — an ACCEPT comment doesn't fix a security bug, and codex is escalating to ensure you don't ship the unfixed surface.
.claude\rules\closed-loop-recursive-narrowing.md:84:When ACCEPT-WITH-DOC's hard-deny on high/critical blocks shipping but the user or named risk-owner explicitly wants the work to land anyway, this is a SEPARATE disposition — not ACCEPT. Future readers must be able to grep for "we shipped a known high/critical defect with explicit acceptance" without that being conflated with "we did our due diligence and bounded the residual risk."
.claude\rules\closed-loop-recursive-narrowing.md:86:Disposition: ship with a `MANUAL-OVERRIDE` marker in the patch site comment AND in the commit/PR body, citing severity, the specific codex finding, and the owner identity. The marker `MANUAL-OVERRIDE` (case-sensitive) signals that NO automated process closed the loop — a human accepted material risk explicitly. Use of this disposition should be rare; track each instance as a code-review-burn metric.
.claude\rules\closed-loop-recursive-narrowing.md:95:- **Confuse ACCEPT with convergence**: shipping an ACCEPT comment on an escalating concern produces *worse* documentation than just removing the feature, because future readers see "we knew this was broken and shipped it anyway"

.claude\rules\parallel-session-worktree-isolation.md:115:   - **(c) Lockfile + O_CREAT|O_APPEND atomic-write for SHARED JSONL append**: open the JSONL log with `os.open(path, os.O_CREAT | os.O_APPEND | os.O_WRONLY, mode)` where `mode` defaults to `0o600` (owner-only — per Round-5b T3 round-3 NEEDS-ATTENTION conf=0.78 NEW-CLASS trust-boundary finding on commit `c2b5dee`: `0o644` was world-readable and leaked audit-trail content (agent prompts, PIDs, verdict cite paths, `agent_id` UUIDs, T1/T2/T3 verdict bodies) on multi-user hosts. Callers MAY opt-in to `0o640` group-readable for shared-CI cases via explicit `mode=` argument + documented umask interaction (e.g., `umask 0o027` for CI runner) — `0o644` is REJECTED as default for any audit-trail JSONL). **Migration semantic for legacy files** *(Round-7 amendment per T3 round-4 NEEDS-ATTENTION conf=0.91 NEW-CLASS finding on commit `df37fb1`; closes non-migrating gap caught by codex GPT-5.5 BRIDGE-MODE — POSIX `os.open` applies `mode` ONLY when `O_CREAT` actually CREATES the file)*: pre-existing files at `0o644` (created under Round-3-through-5 mandates pre-Round-6) RETAIN their world-readable perms after open, leaving the audit-trail leak intact unless coerced. After every `os.open`, the caller MUST: (i) read `current_mode = stat.S_IMODE(os.fstat(fd).st_mode)`; (ii) if `current_mode != mode` AND the file is owned by caller-uid, call `os.fchmod(fd, mode)` to coerce existing file to the mode invariant; (iii) if `os.fchmod` raises (`PermissionError` due to read-only mount, alien owner, ACL conflict on Windows NTFS, etc.), FAIL CLOSED — propagate the exception rather than proceeding with non-conforming perms (the audit-trail invariant is enforced everywhere or fails loudly). Document in commit body for any consumer applying this rule: one-time migration shell command `find .claude/state -name '*.jsonl' -perm /044 -exec chmod 0600 {} +` (POSIX) OR `Get-ChildItem -Path .claude/state -Filter *.jsonl -Recurse | Where-Object { ($_ | Get-Acl).AccessToString -match 'Everyone Allow Read' } | ForEach-Object { icacls $_.FullName /inheritance:r /grant ${env:USERNAME}:F }` (Windows) for legacy `mcp_health.jsonl` / `subagent_transcripts.jsonl` / `codex_postcommit_reviews.jsonl` / `subagent_start.jsonl` / `worktree_lifecycle_audit.jsonl` files created at `0o644` per pre-Round-6 mandates. The `O_CREAT` flag ensures a missing log auto-creates rather than failing the first writer; **if `os.open` raises (read-only mount, permission denied, disk full), the exception MUST propagate — do not catch-and-ignore** (per Round-5 F-1 silent-failure finding). Take an **exclusive advisory lock** (`fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX)` on POSIX / `msvcrt.locking` on Windows); **if neither primitive is available, or if the platform does not enforce advisory locks (e.g., NFS without NLM support), FAIL CLOSED — raise rather than proceeding without a lock** (per Round-5 F-2 NFS-silent-succeed finding). **Windows separate-lockfile mechanism** *(Round-7c per T3 round-7b NEEDS-ATTENTION conf=0.78 NEW-CLASS finding on commit `48c49fb` caught by codex GPT-5.5 BRIDGE-MODE)*: `msvcrt.locking` locks `nbytes` from CURRENT file-pointer position, NOT the whole file like POSIX `fcntl.flock`. Under O_APPEND the JSONL fd's pointer moves on each write, breaking lock-release symmetry (LK_UNLCK at the new pointer would find no lock at the byte LK_LOCK was issued for). Round-7b workaround (shipped at `scripts/_atomic_jsonl_append.py:_acquire_lock(fd, path)` commit `48c49fb`): open separate `<jsonl-path>.lock` file with 1-byte placeholder + lock byte 0 of the LOCKFILE (no writes to lockfile means file pointer stays at byte 0). Module returns `lock_fd` for Windows callers to release; `None` for POSIX. **Lock-protocol rollout constraint** *(Round-7c per same T3 finding)*: when the lock protocol bumps (direct-jsonl-fd → separate-lockfile-v1, or separate-lockfile-v1 → separate-lockfile-v2-versioned), enforce single-version deployment for the entire concurrent-writer cohort. Old + new code locking DIFFERENT lock domains do NOT mutually exclude — concurrent writers can race even though each ALONE acquires its lock correctly. Mitigations (pick ONE before any concurrent rollout): **(i) transitional dual-lock**: acquire both old AND new protocol locks in series during the transition window; **(ii) runtime version-marker**: write protocol-version byte to lockfile + fail-closed on read-version-mismatch (FORWARD-REF for v2 lock protocol bump); **(iii) single-version cohort barrier**: coordinate cohort upgrade via deployment system before any new-version runs. Currently sss has ZERO consumers of `_atomic_jsonl_append.py` (FORWARD-REF wire-up Ships 2-5 pending per `tmp/wave22-orchestrator-salvage-jsonl-mode-bits-audit-2026-05-05.md`), so the version-skew window is THEORETICAL until first hook migrates to use the module. Future protocol bumps MUST honor one of (i)/(ii)/(iii). HOLD the lock across BOTH (a) JSON-encoding the record AND (b) the single low-level `os.write(fd, encoded_bytes)` — never use buffered text writes (`f.write(json.dumps(rec) + "\n")` via Python file objects can split into multiple writes). **If JSON encoding raises (`UnicodeEncodeError`, non-serializable type), release the lock and propagate the exception — do not silently drop the record** (per Round-5 F-3 silent-record-drop finding). For records where **`len(encoded_bytes)` — the byte count AFTER JSON encoding, NOT the key count of the dict —** exceeds the platform atomic-write bound (≤PIPE_BUF 4KB POSIX; ≤512 bytes for Windows or treat the lock as the sole correctness boundary), reject the record OR shard via option (b) filename-namespace; do NOT silently truncate (per Round-5 F-5 measurement-target finding). After the write, `os.fsync(fd)` if durability is part of the contract (audit-trail JSONL needs fsync; ephemeral telemetry may skip); **if `os.fsync` raises (`EIO`, `ENOSPC`), propagate the exception — do not silently ignore a durability failure when durability is contracted** (per Round-5 F-4 fsync-failure finding). Use for SHARED JSONL log targets (`mcp_health.jsonl`, `subagent_transcripts.jsonl`, `codex_postcommit_reviews.jsonl` class) where consumers expect interleaved appends from multiple writers and unified-view semantics are required.

Cite class downgraded to TIER-1-NAMED-AUTHOR-QUOTE-PROVISIONAL with REQUIRED metadata: (a) ISBN/DOI + page + verbatim-quote inline; (b) verifier-identity disclosure (who-verified-when, e.g., `[VERIFIED 2026-05-04 by orchestrator against book Tip #15 verbatim text]`); (c) explicit `non-automatable: true` marker so review hooks know to defer to human sign-off; (d) **HARD-GATE ELIGIBILITY TEST** *(Round-3 amendment a per T3 R3 NEEDS-ATTENTION conf=0.82 same-class finding on commit `1b87a6e`; supersedes round-2 "MUST prefer" soft preference framing — preference is not gateable; eligibility is)*: PROVISIONAL admission is admissible ONLY when DOI landing page + accessible PDF / publisher excerpt / archived scan (license-permitting) was SEARCHED AND UNAVAILABLE. The commit body MUST document the search (which DOI/publisher/archive was queried + return shape — e.g., "searched ACM DOI 10.1145/<doi> 2026-05-05 — paywall-only, no excerpt found; searched Internet Archive — no scan; searched publisher excerpt page — none"). Mere preference is INSUFFICIENT — if any auditable surrogate exists (DOI/PDF/excerpt/scan), use it as the normative source instead of the physical-only book cite. e.g., ACM DOI `https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/<doi>` for ACM papers IS auditable when paywall-free. Secondary aggregator URLs (Wikipedia, `https://pragprog.com/tips/`, `https://martinfowler.com/bliki/<topic>.html`, `c2.com/cgi/wiki`) are VERIFICATION PROXIES only — they help re-verify the primary quote without owning the book physically, but are NOT cited as normative source. **Independent named-reviewer sign-off mandate** *(Round-3 amendment b per T3 R3 NEEDS-ATTENTION conf=0.82 same-class finding on commit `1b87a6e`; supersedes round-2 "Lower-confidence reviewer-sign-off mandate" sole-orchestrator framing — sole-orchestrator verification is no longer admissible)*: rule edits citing TIER-1-NAMED-AUTHOR-QUOTE-PROVISIONAL MUST cite a SECOND verifier-identity BEYOND the orchestrator who replayed the verbatim quote against the source — commit body MUST embed BOTH verifier-identity-1 (the orchestrator, e.g., `[VERIFIED 2026-05-05 by orchestrator against book Tip #15 verbatim text]`) AND verifier-identity-2 (the independent named reviewer, e.g., `[VERIFIED 2026-05-05 by <human-name> against same book + same page + same quote]`) with explicit `[VERIFIED yyyy-mm-dd by <name> against <source>]` markers for each. # Compound Engineering

[![Build Status](https://github.com/EveryInc/compound-engineering-plugin/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/EveryInc/compound-engineering-plugin/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@every-env/compound-plugin)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@every-env/compound-plugin)

AI skills and agents that make each unit of engineering work easier than the last.

## Philosophy

**Each unit of engineering work should make subsequent units easier -- not harder.**

Traditional development accumulates technical debt. Every feature adds complexity. Every bug fix leaves behind a little more local knowledge that someone has to rediscover later. The codebase gets larger, the context gets harder to hold, and the next change becomes slower.

Compound engineering inverts this. 80% is in planning and review, 20% is in execution:

- Plan thoroughly before writing code with `/ce-brainstorm` and `/ce-plan`
- Review to catch issues and calibrate judgment with `/ce-code-review` and `/ce-doc-review`
- Codify knowledge so it is reusable with `/ce-compound`
- Keep quality high so future changes are easy

The point is not ceremony. The point is leverage. A good brainstorm makes the plan sharper. A good plan makes execution smaller. A good review catches the pattern, not just the bug. A good compound note means the next agent does not have to learn the same lesson from scratch.

**Learn more**

- [Full component reference](plugins/compound-engineering/README.md) - all agents and skills
- [Compound engineering: how Every codes with agents](https://every.to/chain-of-thought/compound-engineering-how-every-codes-with-agents)
- [The story behind compounding engineering](https://every.to/source-code/my-ai-had-already-fixed-the-code-before-

# Compounding Engineering Plugin

AI-powered development tools that get smarter with every use. Make each unit of engineering work easier than the last.

## Getting Started

After installing, run `/ce-setup` in any project. It diagnoses your environment, installs missing tools, and bootstraps project config in one interactive flow.

## Components

| Component | Count |
|-----------|-------|
| Agents | 50+ |
| Skills | 38+ |

## Skills

The primary entry points for engineering work, invoked as slash commands. Detailed user-facing documentation for many skills lives in [`docs/skills/`](../../docs/skills/) — each linked skill name below points to its page (purpose, novel mechanics, use cases, chain position). Skills without dedicated docs are still listed; their `SKILL.md` in the source tree is authoritative.

### Core Workflow

`ce-strategy` anchors the loop upstream; `ce-product-pulse` closes it with a read on user outcomes.

| Skill | Description |
|-------|-------------|
| [`/ce-strategy`](../../docs/skills/ce-strategy.md) | Create or maintain `STRATEGY.md` — the product's target problem, approach, persona, key metrics, and tracks. Re-runnable to update. Read as grounding by `/ce-ideate`, `/ce-brainstorm`, and `/ce-plan` when present |
| [`/ce-ideate`](../../docs/skills/ce-ideate.md) | Optional big-picture ideation: generate and critically evaluate grounded ideas, then route the strongest one into brainstorming |
| [`/ce-brainstorm`](../../docs/skills/ce-brainstorm.md) | Interactive Q&A to think through a feature or problem and write a right-sized requirements doc before planning |
| [`/ce-plan`](../../docs/skills/ce-plan.md) | Create structured plans for any multi-step task -- software features, research workflows, events, study plans -- with automatic confidence chec

You can also use your data to build private evals which represent the common LLMs patterns in your workflow without exposing any of that data publicly.\n\nIf you are building with LLMs, creating high quality evals is one of the most impactful things you can do. Without evals, it can be very difficult and time intensive to understand how different model versions might affect your use case. In the words of [OpenAI's President Greg Brockman](https://twitter.com/gdb/status/1733553161884127435):\n\n<img width=\"596\" alt=\"https://x.com/gdb/status/1733553161884127435?s=20\" src=\"https://github.com/openai/evals/assets/35577566/ce7840ff-43a8-4d88-bb2f-6b207410333b\">\n\n## Setup\n\nTo run evals, you will need to set up and specify your [OpenAI API key](https://platform.openai.com/account/api-keys). After you obtain an API key, specify it using the [`OPENAI_API_KEY` environment variable](https://platform.openai.com/docs/quickstart/step-2-setup-your-api-key). Please be aware of the [costs](https://openai.com/pricing) associated with using the API when running evals. You can also run and create evals using [Weights & Biases](https://wandb.ai/wandb_fc/openai-evals/reports/OpenAI-Evals-Demo-Using-W-B-Prompts-to-Run-Evaluations--Vmlldzo0MTI4ODA3).\n\n**Minimum Required Version: Python 3.9**\n\n### Downloading evals\n\nOur evals registry is stored using [Git-LFS](https://git-lfs.com/). Once you have downloaded and installed LFS, you can fetch the evals (from within your local copy of the evals repo) with:\n```sh\ncd evals\ngit lfs fetch --all\ngit lfs pull\n```\n\nThis will populate all the pointer files under `evals/registry/data`.\n\nYou may just want to fetch data for a select eval. You can achieve this via:\n```sh\ngit lfs fetch --include=evals/registry/data/${your eval}\ngit lfs pull\n```\n\n### Making evals\n\nIf you are going to be creating evals, we suggest cloning this repo directly from GitHub and installing the requirements using the following command:\n\n```sh\npip install -e .\n```\n\nUsing `-e`, changes you make to your eval will be reflected immediately without having to reinstall.\n\nOptionally, you can install the formatters for pre-committing with:\n\n```sh\npip install -e .[formatters]\n```\n\nThen run `pre-commit install` to install pre-commit into your git hooks. pre-commit will now run on every commit.\n\nIf you want to manually run all pre-commit hooks on a repository, run `pre-commit run --all-files`. To run individual hooks use `pre-commit run <hook_id>`.\n\n## Running evals\n\nIf you don't want to contribute new evals, but simply want to run them locally, you can install the evals package via pip:\n\n```sh\npip install evals\n```\n\nYou can find the full instructions to run existing evals in [`run-evals.md`](docs/run-evals.md) and our existing eval templates in [`eval-templates.md`](docs/eval-templates.md). For more advanced use cases like prompt chains or tool-using agents, you can use our [Completion Function Protocol](docs/completion-fns.md).\n\nWe provide the option for you to log your eval results to a Snowflake database, if you have one or wish to set one up. For this option, you will further have to specify the `SNOWFLAKE_ACCOUNT`, `SNOWFLAKE_DATABASE`, `SNOWFLAKE_USERNAME`, and `SNOWFLAKE_PASSWORD` environment variables.\n\n## Writing evals\n\nWe suggest getting starting by: \n\n- Walking through the process for building an eval: [`build-eval.md`](docs/build-eval.md)\n- Exploring an example of implementing custom eval logic: [`custom-eval.md`](docs/custom-eval.md)\n- Writing your own completion functions: [`completion-fns.md`](docs/completion-fns.md)\n- Review our starter guide for writing evals: [Getting Started with OpenAI Evals](https://cookbook.openai.com/examples/evaluation/getting_started_with_openai_evals)\n\nPlease note that we are currently not accepting evals with custom code! While we ask you to not submit such evals at the moment, you can still submit model-graded evals with custom model-graded YAML files.\n\nIf you think you have an interesting eval, please open a pull request with your contribution. OpenAI staff actively review these evals when considering improvements to upcoming models.\n\n## FAQ\n\nDo you have any examples of how to build an eval from start to finish?\n\n- Yes! These are in the `examples` folder. We recommend that you also read through [`build-eval.md`](docs/build-eval.md) in order to gain a deeper understanding of what is happening in these examples.\n\nDo you have any examples of evals implemented in multiple different ways?\n\n- Yes! In particular, see `evals/registry/evals/coqa.yaml`. We have implemented small subsets of the [CoQA](https://stanfordnlp.github.io/coqa/) dataset for various eval templates to help illustrate the differences.\n\nWhen I run an eval, it sometimes hangs at the very end (after the final report). What's going on?\n\n- This is a known issue, but you should be able to interrupt it safely and the eval should finish immediately after.\n\nThere's a lot of code, and I just want to spin up a quick eval. Help? OR,\n\nI am a world-class prompt engineer. I choose not to code. How can I contribute my wisdom?\n\n- If you follow an existing [eval template](docs/eval-templates.md) to build a basic or model-graded eval, you don't need to write any evaluation code at all! Just provide your data in JSON format and specify your eval parameters in YAML. Your patch language is a stripped‑down, file‑oriented diff format designed to be easy to parse and safe to apply. You can think of it as a high‑level envelope:\n\n*** Begin Patch\n[ one or more file sections ]\n*** End Patch\n\nWithin that envelope, you get a sequence of file operations.\nYou MUST include a header to specify the action you are taking.\nEach operation starts with one of three headers:\n\n*** Add File: <path> - create a new file. Every following line is a + line (the initial contents).\n*** Delete File: <path> - remove an existing file. Nothing follows.\n*** Update File: <path> - patch an existing file in place (optionally with a rename).\n\nExample patch:\n\n```\n*** Begin Patch\n*** Add File: hello.txt\n+Hello world\n*** Update File: src/app.py\n*** Move to: src/main.py\n@@ def greet():\n-print(\"Hi\")\n+print(\"Hello, world!\")\n*** Delete File: obsolete.txt\n*** End Patch\n```\n\nIt is important to remember:\n\n- You must include a header with your intended action (Add/Delete/Update)\n- You must prefix new lines with `+` even when creating a new file\n\n## `update_plan`\n\nA tool named `update_plan` is available to you. You can use it to keep an up‑to‑date, step‑by‑step plan for the task.\n\nTo create a new plan, call `update_plan` with a short list of 1‑sentence steps (no more than 5-7 words each) with a `status` for each step (`pending`, `in_progress`, or `completed`).\n\nWhen steps have been completed, use `update_plan` to mark each finished step as `completed` and the next step you are working on as `in_progress`. There should always be exactly one `in_progress` step until everything is done. Use this skill for anything in the software delivery lifecycle: writing a PRD ('write a PRD for X', 'let's plan X', 'scope this out'), parsing a PRD into an epic, decomposing an epic into tasks, syncing to GitHub ('sync the X epic', 'push tasks to github'), starting work on an issue ('start working on issue N', 'let's work on issue N'), analyzing parallel work streams, running standups ('standup', 'run the standup'), checking status ('what's next', 'what's blocked', 'what are we working on'), closing issues, or merging an epic. Use ccpm any time the user is talking about shipping a feature, managing work, or tracking progress — even if they don't say 'ccpm' or 'PRD'. Do NOT use for: debugging code, writing tests, reviewing PRs, or raw GitHub issue/PR operations with no delivery context."
